issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ petition seeking to quash communications exchanged between government officers is not maintainable when those communications are not an order affecting the petitioner’s rights.
material_facts: The petition sought to quash communications exchanged between government officers and to prevent interference with the petitioners’ possession and construction.
The communications were inter-departmental and were not orders passed against the petitioners.
The petition was dismissed by the High Court, and the Supreme Court held that it was not maintainable, while treating maintainability as academic because it also considered the merits.
issues.conclusion: A writ petition seeking the stated relief against inter-departmental communications was not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that communications between government officers could not be made the subject matter of the writ petition in the circumstances presented. It did not rely on an earlier case or specify a statutory provision for this conclusion.

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: The claimant brought a petition invoking the court’s constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_quash_internal_officia: The claimant sought to quash communications exchanged internally between government officers.

issues.definition: When a claimant uses a constitutional writ petition to challenge internal official communications, the petition is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Proceedings under a repealed land-ceiling regime abate if the State had not taken possession of the land when the repeal took effect.
material_facts: The land had been declared surplus under the former land-ceiling regime.
The authorities had issued notices directing the tenure holders to surrender possession, but the record did not show that the State had taken actual physical possession.
The former regime was repealed, and the Court addressed the effect of repeal on proceedings where possession had not been taken.
issues.conclusion: All proceedings pending under the former regime abated automatically upon repeal if possession of the land had not been taken by the State.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the repeal legislation and relying on Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P., Ghasitey Lal Sahu v. Competent Authority, Mukarram Ali Khan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Smt. Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport, the Court held that pending proceedings abate upon repeal where the State has not taken possession.

predicates.pending_land_ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding concerning land ceiling remains pending when the former land-ceiling regime is repealed.
predicates.repeal_takes_effect: The repeal of the former land-ceiling regime takes effect.
predicates.state_has_not_taken_possession: The State has not taken possession of the land before the repeal takes effect.

issues.definition: A pending land-ceiling proceeding abates when the former regime is repealed before the State has taken possession.

issues.legal_issue: Transfers of land made in breach of statutory restrictions on surplus land are void, and later transactions derived from a void transfer do not validate it.
material_facts: Final ex parte assessment orders had declared land held by the original tenure holders to be surplus, and those orders had not been challenged.

The original tenure holders transferred land to a housing society after the land-ceiling regime had commenced; the Court accepted the finding that the transfer was prohibited and void under the statutory restrictions.
The alleged sale deed to the housing society and the later deeds in the chain of transfers were not produced, and the appellants did not provide the relevant notification date or supporting details.
The appellants claimed through subsequent transfers and relied on later development of the land.
issues.conclusion: The initial transfer was a void transaction, and the subsequent transactions derived from it had to be ignored.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(1), 5(3), and 10(4) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 restrict transfers of excess vacant land and provide for nullity in the specified circumstances. An action unlawful at its inception cannot be validated by later events; the Court relied on Upen Chandra Gogoi v. State of Assam, Satchidananda Misra v. State of Orissa, Regional Manager, SBI v. Rakesh Kumar Tewari, C. Albert Morris v. K. Chandrasekaran, and Mangal Prasad Tamoli v. Narvadeshwar Mishra.

predicates.land_was_finally_declared_surplus: The land had been finally declared surplus under the applicable land-ceiling process.
predicates.transfer_breached_restrictions_on_surplu: A transfer of the surplus land was made in circumstances in which transfer was prohibited by the applicable restrictions.
predicates.later_claim_derives_from_initial_transfe: A later claimant relies on a chain of transactions originating in the prohibited transfer.

issues.definition: If finally declared surplus land is transferred in breach of restrictions and a later claim depends on that transfer, the initial and derived transfers are ineffective.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising discretionary writ and equitable jurisdiction may refuse relief where the claimant’s case is unsupported, derives from an unlawful transaction, or would frustrate the rights of others or the public interest.
material_facts: The appellants did not produce the alleged sale deeds in the chain of title, and the record did not establish their genuineness or the circumstances of their execution.
The appellants did not join the original tenure holders or subsequent transferees, and no proceedings under the former regime had been initiated against the appellants themselves.
The appellants claimed through a transfer the Court treated as void and sought protection of their possession and construction.
The Court found no special feature warranting equitable relief.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to exercise equitable discretionary jurisdiction in favour of the appellants and dismissed the appeal on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: The power under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and is exercised to advance justice, not to perpetrate legal fraud or unjust gain; a claimant seeking equity must come with clean hands. The Court relied on Champalal Binani v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Chimajirao Kanhojirao Shrike v. Oriental Fire and General Insurance Co., LIC of India v. Asha Goel, State Financial Corporation v. Jagdamba Oil Mills, Chandra Singh v. State of Rajasthan, Punjab Roadways v. Punja Sahib Bus and Transport Co., Sikkim Subba Associates v. State of Sikkim, Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation v. GAR Re-Rolling Mills, M.P. Mittal v. State of Haryana, and State of Maharashtra v. Prabhu.

predicates.constitutional_writ_claim: A claimant asks a court to grant relief in the exercise of constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_unproved_or_unlawful_: The claimant’s asserted title is unsupported by adequate proof or derives from an unlawful transaction.
predicates.relief_would_disregard_competing_rights_: Granting relief would fail to account for the rights of others or the public interest.

issues.definition: A court may refuse equitable writ relief when a claimant relies on unproved or unlawful title and the requested relief would disregard competing rights or the public interest.

issues.legal_issue: A party advancing a fact-dependent claim in a writ proceeding must plead the material facts and provide supporting evidence, and the court need not entertain a claim that is not properly pleaded and proved.
material_facts: The appellants did not produce the alleged sale deeds or provide sufficient pleadings about their execution, the parties to them, or the consideration paid.
The appellants also did not disclose the date of the relevant notification or provide evidence supporting their factual assertions.
The Court held that the appeal lacked the pleadings required for proper adjudication.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not entertain the appellants’ unsupported factual claims.
issues.legal_principle: A party must plead and prove facts required to substantiate a point of law that depends on facts; in a writ petition, the facts and the evidence supporting them must be pleaded and annexed. The Court relied on Bharat Singh v. State of Haryana, Vithal N. Shetti v. Prakash N. Rudrakar, Devasahayam v. P. Savithramma, Sait Nagjee Purushotham & Co. v. Vimalabai Prabhulal, and Rajasthan Pradesh V.S. Sardarshahar v. Union of India.

predicates.writ_proceeding: The claim is made in a writ proceeding.
predicates.claim_depends_on_facts: The legal claim can be decided only by establishing underlying facts.
predicates.claimant_does_not_plead_and_support_mate: The claimant fails to plead the material facts and provide evidence supporting them.

issues.definition: In a writ proceeding, a court need not entertain a fact-dependent claim when the claimant fails to plead and support its material facts.

issues.legal_issue: A court may question parties to ascertain the truth and obtain proper proof of relevant facts, and a party cannot prevent that inquiry merely by asserting that the questions concern matters not in issue.
material_facts: During the appeal, the Court asked the appellants’ counsel questions to ascertain the true facts and the appellants’ bona fides.
Counsel repeatedly responded that the facts the Court sought to ascertain were not in issue.
The Court was unable to elicit the true facts despite its efforts.
issues.conclusion: The Court had power to ask questions to the parties to ascertain the truth, and a party could not insist that the Court’s inquiry was irrelevant or outside the issues.
issues.legal_principle: Section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 empowers a court to ask questions, subject to the provision’s exceptions, to discover or obtain proper proof of facts and secure a just decision. The Court relied on Jamatraj Kewalji Govani v. State of Maharashtra and Zahira Habibulla H. Sheikh v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.court_proceeding: A matter is being heard by a court.
predicates.court_seeks_to_clarify_facts: The court asks a party questions to clarify facts and assist in obtaining proper proof.
predicates.party_objects_only_that_inquiry_is_outsi: A party resists the inquiry solely by asserting that the facts sought are not in issue.

issues.definition: When a court seeks to clarify facts, a party’s assertion that the inquiry is outside the issues does not prevent the court from questioning the parties to ascertain the truth.
